note: Facts and sources behind the member descriptions in MO.json, gathered 2026-10-05. "review" holds research notes for a human check; "issues" lists open questions.

byways.name: Historic Route 66 Byway
byways.designation: Missouri Scenic Byway (also part of the Historic Route 66 National Scenic Byway)
byways.where: Historic US 66 alignment from St. Louis to the Kansas line west of Joplin, on Routes 100, 366, 266, 96, 66 and county and city streets

facts.fact: In Missouri US 66 ran from downtown St. Louis at the Mississippi River to the Kansas state line west of Joplin.
The St. Louis to Springfield road had been a Native American trail known as the Osage Indian Trail; settlers later laid a telegraph line along it and it became the Wire Road.
Missouri was the first state to erect a historic marker on US 66, at Kearney Street and Glenstone Avenue in Springfield.
FHWA lists Historic Route 66 as a National Scenic Byway and All-American Road that includes Missouri.

byways.review: MoDOT links this byway to the Route 66 Association of Missouri rather than to a MoDOT PDF map.

byways.name: Little Dixie Highway of the Great River Road
byways.designation: Missouri Scenic Byway (the Missouri segment of the Great River Road National Scenic Byway)
byways.where: Route 79 along the Mississippi from the Ralls-Pike county line through Louisiana to Clarksville, Pike County

facts.fact: The byway begins on MO 79 at the Ralls-Pike county line 15 miles south of Hannibal and runs 29 miles through Louisiana to Clarksville.
Limestone bluffs line the route, and Clarksville and Louisiana have National Register historic districts.
The Missouri Department of Natural Resources has called Louisiana's the most intact Victorian streetscape in Missouri.
Clarksville, platted in 1819 and named for William Clark, has the Lock and Dam No. 24 Historic District.

byways.review: Not a separate catalog road: it is a short part of the catalog's Great River Road - Missouri (great-river-road-missouri-2247). MoDOT's PDF map labels it a Federal Designated Scenic Byway, and recreation.gov treats it as the Missouri section of the national Great River Road. The MoDOT KML folder also includes short pieces of Routes W, WW and 54.

byways.name: Old Trails Road
byways.where: Route 224 from Lexington west through Wellington and Napoleon to US 24, Lafayette County

facts.fact: Route 224 runs from US 24 near Lexington west to US 24 beyond Napoleon; it follows the Missouri River and is prone to flooding. It was the old US 24 through the towns until a 1959 bypass.
Napoleon and Wellington were named after the commanders at Waterloo, with a crossroads called Waterloo between them.
The 1861 siege of Lexington is also called the Battle of the Hemp Bales.

byways.review: MoDOT publishes one PDF map and one KML folder ('Old Trails and Show Me Sante Fe Trails - Route 224') for this byway and the Show-Me Santa Fe Trail together; Route 224 is the Old Trails Road part.

byways.name: Cliff Drive
byways.where: Cliff Drive and Gladstone Boulevard from The Paseo and Independence Avenue to Belmont Boulevard, Kessler Park, Kansas City

facts.fact: Cliff Drive runs about 4.27 miles through George E. Kessler Park from The Paseo and Independence Avenue to Indian Mound on Gladstone Boulevard at Belmont Boulevard, and was designated a State Scenic Byway on June 2, 2000.
The route preserves limestone bluffs and natural vegetation of the Missouri River valley next to the city core, and is closed to motorized vehicles.
Kessler Park's bluffs overlook the East Bottoms and the Missouri River; the park was a cornerstone of George Kessler's City Beautiful parks and boulevard system.

byways.review: Closed to motorized vehicles per Kansas City Parks.

byways.name: Ozark Mountain Parkway
byways.where: Routes 265 and 248 through Stone County, from near Route 76 north by Reeds Spring and Galena toward the Christian County line

facts.fact: Route 265 is also known as the Ozark Mountain Parkway.
Between Reeds Spring and Galena, Routes 248, 265 and 413 share a winding, hilly two-lane road with switchbacks through the Ozark Mountains, marked no-passing throughout.
At Galena is the Y-Bridge, listed on the National Register of Historic Places and closed to vehicles.

byways.review: MoDOT's PDF map is titled 'Ozark Mountain Byway'. The catalog line is only 1.7 miles, while MoDOT's KML draws roughly 30 miles of Routes 265 and 248.

byways.name: Bloomfield Stars and Stripes Historical/Cultural Byway
byways.where: Routes 25 and AA (with short pieces of E and J) at Bloomfield, Stoddard County

facts.fact: The Stars and Stripes newspaper began in November 1861 when ten Union soldiers, printers by trade, took over a local printing press in Bloomfield.
The Stars and Stripes National Museum and Library in Bloomfield has more than 10,000 square feet of exhibits.
Bloomfield is the Stoddard County seat, on Route 25 about 6.5 miles north of Dexter; its courthouse is on the National Register.

byways.review: MoDOT links the byway to the Stars and Stripes National Museum and Library; no MoDOT PDF map is posted for it.

byways.name: Crowley's Ridge Parkway
byways.designation: Missouri Scenic Byway and National Scenic Byway
byways.where: Route 25 with Routes 62, J and WW through Dunklin County to Malden; continues south into Arkansas

facts.fact: Crowley's Ridge Parkway is a 212-mile National Scenic Byway in northeast Arkansas and the Missouri Bootheel; Missouri granted its designation in 2000 and the route ends at Business Route 25 in Malden.
Crowley's Ridge is a loess ridge rising 250 to 550 feet above the alluvial plain, in a 150-mile line from southeastern Missouri to Helena, Arkansas.
FHWA lists the parkway at 212 miles in Arkansas and Missouri.

byways.review: Wikipedia gives 14.2 miles in Missouri, but MoDOT's KML draws about 40 miles on Routes 25, 62, J and WW south to near the state line.

byways.name: Show-Me Santa Fe Trail
byways.where: US 24 from Lexington east through Dover to Waverly, Lafayette County

facts.fact: The Santa Fe Trail passed north of Marshall, through Lexington to Fort Osage and then Independence.
Dover was platted in 1839 and had 83 residents in 2020.
Waverly is home to Baltimore Bend Winery and was the home of Jo Shelby, a hemp farmer who joined the Confederate cause in 1861.

byways.review: Catalog name is 'Sho-Me Santa Fe Trails' and its line is 9.4 miles; MoDOT's KML draws about 19 miles of US 24 from Lexington to Waverly. MoDOT's map PDF is shared with Old Trails Road.

byways.name: Spirit of Kansas City Regional Scenic Byway
byways.where: West Bottoms and riverfront streets: Woodswether Road, 3rd Street, Berkley Parkway, Grand Boulevard, downtown Kansas City

facts.fact: The West Bottoms lies at the confluence of the Missouri and Kansas rivers, facing Kaw Point, an early Lewis and Clark campsite.
The West Bottoms was founded as a livestock and meatpacking district in 1871; its brick industrial buildings now hold galleries, restaurants and antique shops.
Berkley Riverfront Park lies along the Missouri River at Berkley Parkway and Lydia Avenue, off I-35.

byways.review: No dedicated official page; the URL is MoDOT's Kansas City area byways map PDF.

byways.name: Ozark Mountain Highroad
byways.where: Route 76 (formerly Route 465) from the Route 76 interchange in Stone County to US 65 north of Branson, Stone and Taney counties

facts.fact: The Ozark Mountain Highroad opened in June 2003 as a four-lane freeway through wooded hills northwest of Branson, from Route 76 to US 65, with a ghost-ramp stub south of the Route 76 interchange.
Route 76 was moved onto the Highroad so the city of Branson could take over the strip, and Route 465 was decommissioned with re-signing in early 2020.

byways.review: MoDOT's contacts page still calls it Route 465; the road was re-signed as Route 76 in 2020.

byways.name: Ozark Run Scenic Byway
byways.where: Route 21 from the Big River near Washington State Park south to near the Black River, with Route 8 west to Berryman; Washington and Iron counties

facts.fact: The 78-mile byway starts at the Big River near Washington State Park, reaches west to Courtois Creek in Berryman, and runs south through the St. Francois Mountains and Caledonia, Pilot Knob, Ironton and Arcadia to near the Black River.
The organization calls it Missouri's newest scenic byway, in Iron and Washington counties about 60 miles south of St. Louis.
Fort Davidson at Pilot Knob repulsed Confederate attacks on September 27, 1864; the fort's walls and the crater of its blown magazine are still visible.

byways.review: Newest Missouri byway, not in the catalog. MoDOT has no PDF map for it; its line is in the MoDOT KML.

byways.name: Great River Road - Missouri
byways.designation: Great River Road (Mississippi River Parkway Commission route)
byways.where: Mississippi River corridor from Hannibal through St. Louis, Ste. Genevieve and Cape Girardeau to New Madrid

facts.fact: The Missouri Great River Road runs from Mark Twain's Hannibal past the St. Louis Arch to Ste. Genevieve, Cape Girardeau and New Madrid.
It passes the meeting of the Missouri and Mississippi rivers at St. Charles, and New Madrid's museum covers the 1811 and 1812 earthquakes.

byways.review: MoDOT designates only the Little Dixie stretch on Route 79 in Pike County; the rest of this route is promoted by the Mississippi River Parkway Commission without a Missouri state byway designation.

byways.name: Great River Road
byways.where: Ten-state Mississippi River route; in Missouri FHWA designates it as a National Scenic Byway

facts.fact: The Great River Road follows the Mississippi about 3,000 miles from northern Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico through 10 states; FHWA lists the Missouri portion as a National Scenic Byway.
Recreation.gov describes the Missouri national section as Route 79 from the Ralls-Pike county line to Clarksville.

byways.review: Multi-state catalog entry; the Missouri state member it overlaps is the Little Dixie Highway of the Great River Road.

byways.name: Glade Top Trail
byways.where: Gravel forest roads along ridgetops in the Ava, Cassville and Willow Springs district of Mark Twain National Forest

facts.fact: The 23-mile two-lane all-weather gravel road follows narrow ridgetops about 500 feet above the countryside and is little changed from the road the Civilian Conservation Corps built in the late 1930s.
Seven overlook pull-outs give views northwest to the Springfield Plateau and as far as 40 miles south to the Boston Mountains in Arkansas.
The glades are sunny grassland openings on dolomite bedrock.

byways.name: Blue Buck Knob Scenic Byway
byways.where: Highway AP area and forest roads by Noblett Lake, Ava, Cassville and Willow Springs district of Mark Twain National Forest

facts.fact: The 24-mile byway runs through farmland, open pasture and wooded hillsides, with the Indian Creek and Blue Buck overlooks.
Noblett Lake was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps during the Great Depression; remains of CCC Camp Willow lie on Forest Road 108.

byways.name: Sugar Camp Scenic Byway
byways.where: Highway 112 south of Roaring River State Park, Forest Road 197 and Highway 86 near Cassville, Mark Twain National Forest

facts.fact: The 28-mile drive combines 20 miles of paved highway and an 8-mile gravel section on Forest Road 197, starting from Highway 112 south of Roaring River State Park.
Sugar Camp Fire Tower, off Forest Road 1004, was built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in the 1930s.
Settlers tapped the sugar maples along the route for syrup.

issues: MoDOT's main page says 'ten byways' but the Contacts page lists 11; the extra is the newer Ozark Run Scenic Byway, not in the catalog.

Catalog designations call Old Trails Road, Ozark Mountain Parkway, Ozark Mountain Highroad and Spirit of Kansas City 'State Scenic Backway'; Missouri has no backway category, all eleven are Missouri byways.
Ozark Mountain Parkway catalog line is 1.7 miles; MoDOT KML draws about 30 miles of Routes 265 and 248 in Stone County. Catalog line likely wrong or truncated.
Sho-Me Santa Fe Trails catalog line is 9.4 miles; MoDOT KML draws about 19 miles of US 24 from Lexington to Waverly.
Crowley's Ridge Parkway: Wikipedia says 14.2 miles in Missouri ending at Malden; MoDOT KML draws about 40 miles on Routes 25, 62, J and WW. Check which is current.

Little Dixie Highway of the Great River Road has no catalog entry of its own; it is a short piece of great-river-road-missouri-2247. Recreation.gov describes it as the Missouri section of the national Great River Road, so the national GRR in Missouri may be just this stretch.
Ozark Mountain Highroad: MoDOT contacts still say Route 465; Wikipedia says Route 465 was decommissioned and the road re-signed as Route 76 in 2020.
Cliff Drive is closed to motorized vehicles (Kansas City Parks).
Old Trails Road: no fetched source ties Route 224 to the 1912 National Old Trails Road; the blurb avoids that claim.
Spirit of Kansas City, Old Trails Road, Show-Me Santa Fe Trail, Ozark Mountain Parkway, Ozark Mountain Highroad and Little Dixie have no dedicated web page; their url is MoDOT's PDF map.
missouri66.org works but looks little updated (latest magazine listed is 2016).
